WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The top military and civilian leaders of the U.S. Air Force were forced out Thursday over the handling of nuclear weapons, the Defense Department secretary said. Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Michael Moseley, left, and Secretary Michael Wynne have stepped down. Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael Moseley and Secretary Michael W. Wynne resigned over the department's concern over two incidents, including the August flight of a B-52 bomber that flew across the country with nuclear weapons. "Focus of the Air Force leadership has drifted" in terms of handling nuclear weapons and equipment, Defense Secretary Robert Gates said. In August, a B-52 bomber flew from North Dakota to Louisiana with the crew unaware that six nuclear-tipped missiles were on board. Four officers were relieved of duty afterward, including three colonels. Gates also cited this year's discovery that components designed to arm and fuse nuclear warheads were accidentally shipped to Taiwan in 2006.  Watch Gates talk about the firings » . Critics also cite last month's news that the Air Force's 5th Bomb Wing failed a defense "nuclear surety" inspection -- despite having months to prepare and being under close scrutiny after the previous incidents. The inspection found deficiencies in the wing's ability to protect its part of the nation's nuclear stockpile. The resignations come after a report on a Navy admiral's investigation that criticized the Air Force's reactions to the incidents. Gates said the report "depicts a pattern of poor performance" in which Air Force brass didn't act to improve security after mishaps and Air Force personnel handling nuclear weapons consistently failed to follow existing rules. Air Force leaders "not only fell short in terms of specific acts, they failed to recognize systemic problems, to address those problems or, when beyond their authority to act, to call the attention of superiors to those problems," Gates said. The investigation found that although the Taiwan incident didn't compromise the integrity of the U.S. nuclear force, it represented "a significant failure" by the Air Force to ensure sensitive military components, Gates said. Gates said the report concluded that erosion in the branch's command and oversight standards helped lead to the incidents, and that they could have been prevented if the oversight programs had functioned correctly. He said he asked for the resignations after consulting President Bush. Sen. Carl Levin, the Democratic chairman of the Senate Armed Service committee, welcomed Gates' decision. "Secretary Gates' focus on accountability is essential and had been absent from the office of the Secretary of Defense for too long," Levin said. "The safety and security of America's nuclear weapons must receive the highest priority, just as it must in other countries." Rep. Edward J. Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat and a senior member of the House Homeland Security Committee, also welcomed the resignations. Markey said he's long been concerned about what he called a series of dangerous Air Force missteps in handling nuclear weapons. "The magnitude and frequency of these errors indicate a deep-seated problem within Air Force culture, practice and training," Markey said. "The entire Department of Defense should immediately recommit itself to ensuring the safety and security of our nuclear stockpile before one of these mistakes has lethal consequences." A senior military source said the August nuclear weapons incident was the straw that broke the camel's back but that other leadership issues also factored into Moseley's and Wynne's resignations. A previous investigation into the B-52 flight uncovered a "lackadaisical" attention to detail in day-to-day operations at the air bases involved, an Air Force official said in October. Maj. Gen. Dick Newton, assistant deputy chief of staff for operations, said the investigation found "a failure to follow procedures" by "a limited number of airmen" at the two bases. Newton defended the procedures themselves. Wynne is not the first secretary of a military branch to resign since Gates became Defense secretary. In March 2007, Gates announced the resignation of Army Secretary Francis J. Harvey in the wake of reports of substandard conditions at Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington. CNN's Jamie McIntyre and Barbara Starr contributed to this report.

outputs.L1:
WASHINGTON (CNN) — The top military and civilian leaders of the U.S. Air Force were forced out Thursday over the handling of nuclear weapons, Defense Secretary Robert Gates said.

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael Moseley and Air Force Secretary Michael W. Wynne resigned amid Defense Department concerns over two incidents, including an August flight in which a B-52 bomber traveled across the country carrying nuclear weapons.

Gates said the “focus of the Air Force leadership has drifted” with respect to the handling of nuclear weapons and related equipment.

In August, a B-52 bomber flew from North Dakota to Louisiana while its crew was unaware that six nuclear-tipped missiles were on board. Four officers, including three colonels, were relieved of duty afterward.

Gates also cited the discovery this year that components designed to arm and fuse nuclear warheads had been accidentally shipped to Taiwan in 2006.

Critics have also pointed to news last month that the Air Force’s 5th Bomb Wing failed a Defense Department “nuclear surety” inspection, despite having months to prepare and being under close scrutiny following the earlier incidents. The inspection found deficiencies in the wing’s ability to protect its portion of the nation’s nuclear stockpile.

The resignations followed a report on an investigation by a Navy admiral that criticized the Air Force’s response to the incidents. Gates said the report “depicts a pattern of poor performance,” in which senior Air Force officials failed to improve security after mishaps and Air Force personnel responsible for handling nuclear weapons consistently failed to follow existing rules.

Air Force leaders “not only fell short in terms of specific acts, they failed to recognize systemic problems, to address those problems or, when beyond their authority to act, to call the attention of superiors to those problems,” Gates said.

The investigation found that, although the Taiwan incident did not compromise the integrity of the U.S. nuclear force, it represented “a significant failure” by the Air Force to ensure the security of sensitive military components, Gates said.

Gates said the report concluded that an erosion of the branch’s command and oversight standards contributed to the incidents and that they could have been prevented had oversight programs functioned properly. He said he requested the resignations after consulting President Bush.

Sen. Carl Levin, the Democratic chairman of the Senate Armed Services Committee, welcomed Gates’ decision.

“Secretary Gates’ focus on accountability is essential and had been absent from the office of the Secretary of Defense for too long,” Levin said. “The safety and security of America’s nuclear weapons must receive the highest priority, just as it must in other countries.”

Rep. Edward J. Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat and senior member of the House Homeland Security Committee, also welcomed the resignations. Markey said he had long been concerned about what he described as a series of dangerous Air Force missteps in the handling of nuclear weapons.

“The magnitude and frequency of these errors indicate a deep-seated problem within Air Force culture, practice and training,” Markey said. “The entire Department of Defense should immediately recommit itself to ensuring the safety and security of our nuclear stockpile before one of these mistakes has lethal consequences.”

A senior military source said the August nuclear weapons incident was the straw that broke the camel’s back, but that other leadership issues also contributed to Moseley’s and Wynne’s resignations.

A previous investigation into the B-52 flight uncovered “lackadaisical” attention to detail in day-to-day operations at the air bases involved, an Air Force official said in October.

Maj. Gen. Dick Newton, assistant deputy chief of staff for operations, said the investigation found “a failure to follow procedures” by “a limited number of airmen” at the two bases. Newton defended the procedures themselves.

Wynne is not the first secretary of a military branch to resign since Gates became Defense secretary. In March 2007, Gates announced the resignation of Army Secretary Francis J. Harvey following reports of substandard conditions at Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington.

CNN’s Jamie McIntyre and Barbara Starr contributed to this report.

Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael Moseley and Air Force Secretary Michael W. Wynne submitted their resignations after Defense Department concerns about two major incidents. One involved an August flight in which a B-52 bomber traveled across the United States carrying nuclear weapons. Defense Secretary Robert Gates said the Air Force leadership’s attention to the handling of nuclear arms and related equipment had “drifted.”

In that August incident, a B-52 flew from North Dakota to Louisiana while its crew did not know that six missiles armed with nuclear warheads were aboard. Afterward, four officers, including three colonels, were removed from their positions.

Gates also pointed to the discovery earlier this year that parts used to arm and fuse nuclear warheads had mistakenly been sent to Taiwan in 2006.

Critics have also noted that the Air Force’s 5th Bomb Wing failed a Defense Department “nuclear surety” inspection last month, even though the unit had months to get ready and was already receiving heightened attention because of the earlier problems. Inspectors found weaknesses in the wing’s capacity to safeguard its portion of the U.S. nuclear arsenal.

The departures followed a report based on an investigation led by a Navy admiral, which faulted the Air Force’s response to the incidents. Gates said the report showed “a pattern of poor performance,” including senior Air Force officials failing to improve security after mistakes and personnel who handled nuclear weapons repeatedly not following established procedures.

According to Gates, Air Force leaders “not only fell short in terms of specific acts,” but also failed to identify broader systemic issues, correct them, or alert higher-ranking officials when the problems were outside their authority to fix.

The inquiry concluded that the Taiwan shipment did not damage the reliability or integrity of the U.S. nuclear force, but it still amounted to “a significant failure” by the Air Force to properly control sensitive military parts, Gates said.

Gates said the report determined that a weakening of command standards and oversight within the service contributed to the incidents. He added that the problems could have been avoided if the oversight systems had worked as intended. Gates said he requested the resignations after speaking with President Bush.

Sen. Carl Levin, the Michigan Democrat who chaired the Senate Armed Services Committee, praised Gates’ action. “Secretary Gates’ focus on accountability is essential and had been absent from the office of the Secretary of Defense for too long,” Levin said. “The safety and security of America’s nuclear weapons must receive the highest priority, just as it must in other countries.”

Rep. Edward J. Markey, a Massachusetts Democrat and senior member of the House Homeland Security Committee, also supported the resignations. Markey said he had been worried for some time about what he described as a pattern of dangerous Air Force errors in the handling of nuclear weapons.

“The magnitude and frequency of these errors indicate a deep-seated problem within Air Force culture, practice and training,” Markey said. “The entire Department of Defense should immediately recommit itself to ensuring the safety and security of our nuclear stockpile before one of these mistakes has lethal consequences.”

A senior military source said the August nuclear weapons episode was the final breaking point, though other leadership concerns also contributed to the departures of Moseley and Wynne.

An earlier investigation into the B-52 flight found what an Air Force official in October described as a “lackadaisical” approach to details in routine operations at the bases involved. Maj. Gen. Dick Newton, assistant deputy chief of staff for operations, said that review found “a failure to follow procedures” by “a limited number of airmen” at the two bases, while also defending the procedures themselves.

Wynne was not the first military service secretary to resign during Gates’ tenure as defense secretary. In March 2007, Gates announced that Army Secretary Francis J. Harvey was stepping down after reports exposed poor conditions at Walter Reed Army Medical Center in Washington.

CNN’s Jamie McIntyre and Barbara Starr contributed to the report.

**WASHINGTON (CNN-style)** — Defense Secretary Robert Gates has forced the resignations of the Air Force’s top civilian and uniformed leaders following a series of serious failures involving the handling of nuclear weapons and related components, Pentagon officials said.

Air Force Secretary Michael Wynne and Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Michael Moseley were asked to step down after investigations found deep problems in the service’s oversight of its nuclear mission.

The move followed two major incidents that embarrassed the Air Force and raised concerns at the highest levels of the Pentagon. In one case, a B-52 bomber mistakenly carried nuclear-armed cruise missiles from Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana in 2007. The weapons were not properly accounted for during the flight, and officials later said procedures for tracking and safeguarding them had broken down.

In another incident, the Defense Department disclosed that nuclear missile components had been mistakenly shipped to Taiwan. The parts were sent instead of helicopter batteries and remained there for an extended period before the error was discovered.

Gates said the incidents pointed to a decline in standards and accountability within the Air Force’s nuclear enterprise. The resignations were intended to signal that the Pentagon considered the failures systemic, not isolated mistakes by lower-ranking personnel.

The Air Force has long been responsible for a major portion of the nation’s nuclear deterrent, including intercontinental ballistic missiles and nuclear-capable bombers. The mishandling of nuclear weapons and related technology is considered among the most serious security failures in the military.

Wynne, the Air Force’s civilian chief, had served as secretary since 2005. Moseley, a four-star general and former fighter pilot, had served as chief of staff since 2005 and was the service’s highest-ranking uniformed officer.

The shake-up came as the Air Force was already under scrutiny over management, weapons acquisition programs and internal disputes with Pentagon leadership. But officials said the nuclear weapons failures were the central reason for Gates’ decision.

The Pentagon ordered a series of reviews and corrective actions after the incidents, including stricter inventory controls, renewed training and changes in command oversight. Several officers and enlisted personnel were disciplined after the B-52 episode, but Gates’ decision to remove the service’s top leaders marked a far broader judgment about responsibility.

The resignations represented one of the most dramatic accountability moves involving senior military leadership in years and underscored the Pentagon’s view that nuclear weapons require the highest level of discipline, precision and command attention.

**BREAKING NEWS: Gates Removes Top Air Force Leaders After Nuclear Weapons and Taiwan Shipment Blunders**

**WASHINGTON —** Defense Secretary Robert M. Gates has ousted the two highest-ranking civilian and military leaders of the U.S. Air Force, citing a breakdown in accountability and oversight following a series of serious mishandlings of sensitive military equipment, including the mistaken flight of nuclear-armed missiles across the United States and the erroneous shipment of nuclear weapons-related components to Taiwan.

Gates announced Thursday that he had accepted the resignations of Air Force Secretary Michael W. Wynne and Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. T. Michael Moseley, marking one of the most dramatic leadership shake-ups in the modern history of the service.

The decision follows months of investigations into the Air Force’s handling of nuclear weapons and related materials. The most prominent incident occurred in August 2007, when a B-52 bomber flew from Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana carrying cruise missiles that had mistakenly been armed with nuclear warheads. The weapons were not properly accounted for during the flight, and senior officials later described the episode as a grave failure of nuclear surety procedures.

A separate and equally alarming incident involved the mistaken shipment of electrical fuses used in intercontinental ballistic missile nose cones to Taiwan. The parts were sent instead of helicopter batteries that Taiwan had ordered. The shipment went undetected for an extended period, raising concerns not only about inventory controls but also about the handling of sensitive nuclear-related technology in the international supply chain.

At a Pentagon news conference, Gates said the incidents revealed “a pattern of poor performance” and a failure by Air Force leadership to maintain the highest standards required for nuclear weapons stewardship.

“These events did not occur in isolation,” Gates said. “They point to systemic problems in the Air Force’s attention to detail, discipline, and accountability in its nuclear mission.”

Gates stressed that the United States’ nuclear arsenal remained safe and secure, but he made clear that the errors had damaged confidence in the Air Force’s management of one of the military’s most sensitive responsibilities.

The removal of Wynne and Moseley is highly unusual. Service secretaries and chiefs of staff are rarely forced out simultaneously, and the move underscores the seriousness with which Gates and other senior defense officials viewed the lapses.

The Air Force had already faced scrutiny after the B-52 incident, which shocked officials because of the strict procedures normally surrounding nuclear weapons. Nuclear warheads are supposed to be tracked under multiple layers of verification, custody, and command control. The fact that armed missiles could be loaded onto an aircraft and flown across the country without immediate detection prompted investigations, disciplinary actions, and a broad review of nuclear handling procedures.

The Taiwan shipment further intensified concerns. Though the components were not nuclear warheads and did not constitute a nuclear weapon, they were associated with nuclear delivery systems. Their accidental shipment to a foreign government raised questions about the reliability of military logistics systems and triggered diplomatic sensitivities, particularly because of Taiwan’s relationship with China.

Gates commissioned a high-level review led by Navy Adm. Kirkland H. Donald, director of the Naval Nuclear Propulsion Program. That review found shortcomings in Air Force procedures, training, inspection systems, and command oversight related to nuclear matters.

According to defense officials, the review concluded that the problems extended beyond isolated mistakes by lower-level personnel and reflected broader institutional failures.

Wynne, the Air Force’s top civilian official, had served as secretary since 2005. Moseley, the service’s top uniformed officer, became chief of staff the same year. Both men had also been involved in policy debates with Gates over Air Force priorities, including the balance between traditional airpower missions and the immediate needs of ground forces in Iraq and Afghanistan.

While Gates emphasized the nuclear-related incidents as the reason for the removals, the decision also comes amid broader tensions between the Pentagon leadership and the Air Force over budgets, modernization programs, and the service’s role in current wars.

The Air Force had been pressing for more funding to replace aging aircraft and expand programs such as advanced fighter jets. Gates, however, repeatedly urged the services to focus more directly on the wars then underway, including increasing the supply of intelligence, surveillance, and reconnaissance assets such as unmanned aerial vehicles.

Still, Pentagon officials said the decisive issue was accountability for failures in nuclear stewardship.

The shake-up is expected to prompt major reforms within the Air Force’s nuclear enterprise. Gates said the Pentagon would implement recommendations from the nuclear review and strengthen oversight of weapons handling, inventory management, training, and inspection procedures.

The resignations also send a clear message across the armed forces that senior leaders will be held responsible for institutional failures, particularly in missions involving nuclear weapons.

The United States has long treated nuclear weapons management as a no-fail mission, governed by stringent safety and security protocols. The Minot-Barksdale flight and the Taiwan shipment were seen as breaches of that culture and prompted alarm both inside and outside the Pentagon.

Members of Congress are expected to seek further briefings on the firings and on the corrective measures being put in place. Lawmakers from both parties previously criticized the Air Force for the incidents and demanded assurances that similar failures could not happen again.

Gates did not immediately name permanent successors for Wynne and Moseley, but interim leadership arrangements are expected while the White House and Pentagon consider replacements.

The move represents a defining moment in Gates’s tenure as defense secretary and a major rebuke of Air Force leadership. It also places renewed focus on the military’s nuclear mission at a time when the United States is engaged in wars overseas and managing complex security relationships around the world.

For the Air Force, the departures of Wynne and Moseley signal the beginning of a difficult internal reckoning over how deeply nuclear oversight problems had taken root — and how quickly the service can restore confidence in its ability to manage the nation’s most powerful weapons.

WASHINGTON (CNN) -- The Pentagon announced sweeping accountability actions after a series of nuclear surety failures in the Air Force exposed what senior defense officials described as a breakdown in discipline, oversight and command attention across the service’s nuclear enterprise.

The actions follow multiple high-profile incidents involving nuclear weapons and nuclear-related components, including the unauthorized transfer of nuclear-armed cruise missiles across the United States and the mistaken shipment of sensitive missile parts overseas. Together, the failures prompted a broad review of Air Force procedures and led Defense Department leaders to conclude that the problems were not isolated mistakes but symptoms of deeper institutional neglect.

Senior Pentagon officials said the measures are intended to restore confidence in the military’s handling of nuclear weapons, one of its most sensitive responsibilities. The steps include disciplinary action against commanders and personnel involved in the incidents, changes in inspection and certification procedures, and a renewed emphasis on nuclear surety training throughout the Air Force.

“The stewardship of nuclear weapons demands the highest standards of accountability,” a senior defense official said. “When those standards are not met, the department has an obligation to act decisively.”

The most serious incident occurred when a B-52 bomber was mistakenly loaded with nuclear-armed cruise missiles and flown from Minot Air Force Base in North Dakota to Barksdale Air Force Base in Louisiana. The weapons were supposed to have been removed from service and transported without nuclear warheads. Instead, they remained mounted on the aircraft for hours before the error was discovered.

Although officials said the weapons were never at risk of detonation and remained under military control, the incident alarmed lawmakers and defense experts because it suggested multiple safeguards had failed. Procedures designed to track, verify and secure nuclear weapons were either ignored or improperly carried out.

In a separate episode, components associated with ballistic missile systems were mistakenly shipped to Taiwan. The parts were not nuclear warheads, but their transfer raised concerns about inventory controls, communication within the supply system and the handling of sensitive military equipment.

Defense officials said those incidents triggered a series of investigations, including internal Air Force reviews and outside assessments directed by the Pentagon. The reviews found weaknesses in leadership focus, training, inspections and logistics management. In particular, investigators concluded that the Air Force had allowed its nuclear mission to lose prominence as attention shifted to conventional operations in Iraq, Afghanistan and other global commitments.

The accountability actions reach across several levels of command. Officers and enlisted personnel directly involved in mishandling weapons or failing to follow procedures have faced administrative or disciplinary measures. Some commanders have been relieved, while others received letters of reprimand or other career-impacting sanctions.

At the senior leadership level, Pentagon officials said the failures required a broader response. The department moved to restructure oversight of nuclear operations, strengthen command responsibility and ensure that nuclear surety receives sustained attention from top Air Force leaders.

Defense analysts said the Pentagon’s response reflects the gravity of the nuclear mission.

“In most military operations, mistakes can be serious but recoverable,” said one former senior defense official familiar with nuclear policy. “With nuclear weapons, the margin for error is essentially zero. The system depends on precision, redundancy and a culture that treats every procedure as mandatory.”

Members of Congress from both parties have pressed the Pentagon for answers, arguing that the incidents damaged public trust and could undermine U.S. credibility abroad. Lawmakers have called for regular updates on corrective actions and have urged the Defense Department to ensure that responsibility does not stop at lower-ranking personnel.

Pentagon leaders have emphasized that the nation’s nuclear arsenal remains safe, secure and reliable. But they also acknowledged that confidence in the system depends not only on physical security but on rigorous accountability.
